parts.problem_md:
Phenol can be prepared from phenylamine.

There are three stages that take place during this preparation:

- **Stage 1:** Prepare nitric(III) acid using sodium nitrate and hydrochloric acid
- **Stage 2:** React phenylamine with nitric(III) acid and hydrochloric acid to form a diazonium salt
- **Stage 3:** Thermal decomposition of the diazonium salt to form phenol, hydrochloric acid, and nitrogen gas

i) State the essential conditions for the reaction in **stage 2**.

[1]

ii) Draw the skeletal formula of the diazonium salt formed in **stage 2**.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The essential conditions for the reaction in stage 2 are:
> 
> - Temperature below 10 °C **[1 mark]**

ii) The skeletal formula of the diazonium salt formed in stage 2 is:

![Skeletal formula of benzenediazonium chloride showing a phenyl group bonded to a diazonium group with a positive charge and a chloride counter ion](assets/001-skeletal-formula-of-benzenediazonium-chloride-sh.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>– group bonded to nitrogen
> 
> 1 mark for N≡N<sup>+</sup> group shown
> 
> 1 mark for Cl<sup>-</sup> counter ion

> **[exam-tip]**
> The temperature is kept below 10 °C to prevent the diazonium salt decomposing prematurely.
> 
> The diazonium salt formed in stage 2 is benzenediazonium chloride. The diazotisation reaction is:
> 
> C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + HNO<sub>2</sub> + HCl → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>-</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Phenol can be prepared from phenylamine.

There are three stages that take place during this preparation:

- **Stage 1:** Prepare nitric(III) acid using sodium nitrate and hydrochloric acid
- **Stage 2:** React phenylamine with nitric(III) acid and hydrochloric acid to form a diazonium salt
- **Stage 3:** Thermal decomposition of the diazonium salt to form phenol, hydrochloric acid, and nitrogen gas

Construct balanced equations for the reactions that occur at each stage.

Stage 1:

Stage 2:

Stage 3:
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The balanced equations for each stage are:
> 
> Stage 1:
> 
> - NaNO<sub>2</sub> + HCl → HNO<sub>2</sub> + NaCl **[1 mark]**
> 
> Stage 2:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + HNO<sub>2</sub> + HCl → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>-</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O
> **OR**
> C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + NaNO<sub>2</sub> + 2HCl → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>-</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + NaCl **[1 mark]**
> 
> Stage 3:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + HCl + N<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Stage 1: sodium nitrite reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce nitric(III) acid (nitrous acid) and sodium chloride.
> 
> Stage 2: phenylamine undergoes diazotisation with nitric(III) acid and hydrochloric acid to form benzenediazonium chloride and water. The reaction also occurs directly with sodium nitrite and excess hydrochloric acid. In this case sodium chloride is also produced.
> 
> Stage 3: the diazonium salt undergoes thermal decomposition in the presence of water to give phenol, hydrochloric acid, and nitrogen gas.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Phenol can be prepared from phenylamine.

There are three stages that take place during this preparation:

- **Stage 1:** Prepare nitric(III) acid using sodium nitrate and hydrochloric acid
- **Stage 2:** React phenylamine with nitric(III) acid and hydrochloric acid to form a diazonium salt
- **Stage 3:** Thermal decomposition of the diazonium salt to form phenol, hydrochloric acid, and nitrogen gas

The diazonium salt formed during stage 2 can also react with phenol to form a useful substance, **Z**.

i) Draw the skeletal formula of **Z**.

[2]

ii) Suggest a possible use for **Z**.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) The skeletal formula of Z is:

![Skeletal formula of an azo dye showing two phenyl rings linked by an N=N azo group, with a hydroxyl group on one ring](assets/002-skeletal-formula-of-an-azo-dye-showing-two-pheny.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for both arene rings and hydroxyl group (–OH) correctly drawn and connected
> 
> 1 mark for –N=N– azo group connecting the two rings
> 
> ii) A possible use for Z is:
> 
> Any **one** from
> 
> - Dye
> - Food colouring
> - Indicator
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Azo dyes are formed from the reaction between diazonium ions and phenol in a coupling reaction.
> 
> In this reaction, an orange dye is formed.
> 
> Make sure you are able to draw the structure of this azo compound.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Phenol can be prepared from phenylamine.

There are three stages that take place during this preparation:

- **Stage 1:** Prepare nitric(III) acid using sodium nitrate and hydrochloric acid
- **Stage 2:** React phenylamine with nitric(III) acid and hydrochloric acid to form a diazonium salt
- **Stage 3:** Thermal decomposition of the diazonium salt to form phenol, hydrochloric acid, and nitrogen gas

The first step of substance Z involves creating the diazonium ion.

The reaction is the same as that in stage 2 in part **(a)**.

Explain why the reaction to produce the diazonium ion is carried out at below 10 <sup>o</sup>C.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reaction to produce the diazonium ion is carried out below 10 °C because:
> 
> - The diazonium ion will decompose at higher temperatures **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In the next step, the diazonium ion is reacted with phenol in a coupling reaction to form the azo compound Z.
> 
> Keeping the temperature below 10 °C prevents the diazonium ion from decomposing before it can react with phenol.
> 
> Decomposition of the diazonium ion produces phenol and nitrogen gas.

parts.problem_md:
1-naphthol is a phenolic compound. Its structure is shown in Fig. 3.1.

![Skeletal formula of naphthol](assets/003-skeletal-formula-of-naphthol.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Deduce the molecular formula of 1-naphthol.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The molecular formula of 1-naphthol is:
> 
> - C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> It can be useful to sketch 1-naphthol showing all hydrogen atoms explicitly before counting.
> 
> A common mistake is to assume there are 12 carbon atoms because there appear to be two benzene rings. However, two carbon atoms are shared between the fused rings, giving a total of 10 carbons.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

1-naphthol is a phenolic compound. Its structure is shown in Fig. 3.1.

The molecular formula of 1-naphthol is: C10H8O

Like phenol, 1-naphthol is a weak acid.

Construct an equation to show how 1-naphthol acts as a weak acid.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> An equation to show how 1-naphthol acting as a weak acid is:
> 
> - C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>7</sub>OH ⇌ C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>7</sub>O<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup>
> **OR**
>  C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>7</sub>OH + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>7</sub>O<sup>-</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Both correct formulae and the equilibrium sign (⇌) are required for this mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> You would not be penalised for omitting square brackets around the naphtholate anion. The square brackets indicate that the negative charge is delocalised across the whole ion, as a lone pair on the oxygen atom overlaps with the delocalised π system of the ring.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

1-naphthol is a phenolic compound. Its structure is shown in Fig. 3.1.

![Skeletal formula of naphthol](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/04/7-4-3a-e-1-naphthol-a.png)

Fig. 3.1

1-naphthol undergoes similar reactions to phenol.

Suggest the structure of the organic compound produced when 1-naphthol reacts with bromine water.
parts.solution_md:
The structure of the organic compound produced when 1-naphthol reacts with bromine water is:

![Skeletal formula of the product from the bromination of 1-naphthol](assets/004-skeletal-formula-of-the-product-from-the-bromina.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct dibrominated product of 1-naphthol

> **[exam-tip]**
> When phenol reacts with bromine water, 2,4,6-tribromophenol is produced. The –OH group is an activating group that directs incoming electrophiles to the 2, 4 and 6 positions.
> 
> A similar reaction occurs with 1-naphthol, but position 6 is not available (there is no hydrogen atom on that carbon to be replaced), so bromination occurs at positions 2 and 4 to give 2,4-dibromo-1-naphthol.

parts.problem_md:
Rodinol can be synthesised from phenol by the following route:

![Reaction scheme from phenol via an intermediate to the final product of rodinol](assets/005-reaction-scheme-from-phenol-via-an-intermediate-.png)

i) State the reagents and conditions for step **1**.

[1]

ii) Name the reaction mechanism for step **1**.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents and conditions for step **1** are:
> 
> - Dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> / HNO<sub>3</sub> (aq)
> **AND**
> Room temperature **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The name of the reaction mechanism for step **1** is:
> 
> - Electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Step 1 is the nitration of phenol. Unlike benzene nitration (which requires concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>), phenol reacts with dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> at room temperature because the –OH group activates the ring. Concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> would give 2,4,6-trinitrophenol.
> 
> The product shown has the nitro group at position 4, which is one of the two expected products (along with the 2-nitro isomer).

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Rodinol can be synthesised from phenol by the following route:

![Reaction scheme from phenol via an intermediate to the final product of rodinol](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2026/06/43076-rodinol-reaction-scheme.png)

i) State the type of reaction that occurs in step **2**.

[1]

ii) State the reagents and conditions for step **2**.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of reaction that occurs in step **2** is:
> 
> - Reduction **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The reagents and conditions for step **2** are:
> 
> - Sn / HCl **[1 mark]**
> - Heat under reflux **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Step 2 converts the nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>) to an amine (–NH<sub>2</sub>), which is a reduction reaction. Tin (Sn) acts as the reducing agent in the presence of HCl, and heat under reflux provides the energy needed.
> 
> Under acidic conditions the amine product is protonated (–NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>), so excess NaOH may be added afterwards to give the free amine (–NH<sub>2</sub>).

parts.problem_md:
Rodinol can undergo many reactions.

Draw the skeletal formulae of compounds **E**, **F** and **G** from the reaction chart of rodinol shown below.

![Reaction scheme of rodinol (aminophenol) forming products E with NaOH, G with aqueous bromine, and overall product F on treatment with hydrochloric acid](assets/006-reaction-scheme-of-rodinol-aminophenol-forming-p.png)
parts.solution_md:
The skeletal formulae of compounds **E**, **F** and **G **are:

Compound **E**:

![Structural formula of sodium 4-aminophenoxide, showing a benzene ring with para amino and sodium phenoxide substituents](assets/007-structural-formula-of-sodium-4-aminophenoxide-sh.png)

Compound **F**:

![Structural formula of para-phenylenediamine hydrochloride, showing a benzene ring with NH₂ and protonated NH₃⁺ groups opposite, plus Cl⁻ counter-ion](assets/008-structural-formula-of-para-phenylenediamine-hydr.png)

Compound **G**:

![Structural diagram of a benzene ring labelled with OH on top, NH₂ below, and two Br atoms on left and right, showing 4-amino-2,6-dibromophenol.](assets/009-structural-diagram-of-a-benzene-ring-labelled-wi.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of **E**: H<sub>2</sub>N–C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>–O<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of **F**: HO–C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>–NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>-</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of **G**: HO–C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>2</sub>Br<sub>2</sub>–NH<sub>2</sub>
> 
> Further substitution of **G** to form HO–C<sub>6</sub>HBr<sub>3</sub>–NH<sub>2</sub> **OR** HO–C<sub>6</sub>Br<sub>4</sub>–NH<sub>2</sub> is accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Rodinol is a weak acid (phenol group) and a base (amine group):
> 
> - Reaction with NaOH: the phenol –OH is deprotonated to give compound E (sodium 4-aminophenoxide) and water
> - Reaction with HCl: the –NH<sub>2</sub> is protonated to give compound F (4-aminophenol hydrochloride)
> 
> When rodinol reacts with excess aqueous bromine, both the –OH and –NH<sub>2</sub> groups are activating, directing electrophiles to positions 2 and 6. The most likely product (compound G) is 4-amino-2,6-dibromophenol, but further bromination is also possible and accepted.

parts.problem_md:
Phenol behaves as a weak acid.

i) Construct the equation for the reaction of phenol with sodium hydroxide.

[1]

ii) Construct the equation for the reaction of phenol with sodium metal.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of phenol with sodium hydroxide is:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + NaOH → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the reaction of phenol with sodium metal is:
> 
> - 2C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 2Na → 2C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> These are acid–base reactions:
> 
> Acid + base → salt + water (phenol + NaOH)
> 
> Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas (phenol + Na)
> 
> The product in both reactions is sodium phenoxide, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>. The phenoxide ion (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>) forms an ionic bond with Na<sup>+</sup>.

parts.problem_md:
Phenol undergoes electrophilic substitution when reacted with bromine water at room temperature.

State **two** observations that can be made during this reaction.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Two observations when phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature:
> 
> - The bromine water decolourises (from orange to colourless) **[1 mark]**
> - A white precipitate forms **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The orange bromine water decolourises as bromine is consumed in the reaction. The white precipitate is 2,4,6-tribromophenol, which is insoluble in water.

parts.problem_md: Draw the skeletal formulae of the two possible products from the reaction of phenol with **dilute** nitric acid.
parts.solution_md:
The skeletal formulae of the two possible products are:

![2 and 4 nitrophenol ](assets/010-2-and-4-nitrophenol.jpeg)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for each correct skeletal formula (2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol)

> **[exam-tip]**
> When phenol reacts with dilute nitric acid, the two products are 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol. When concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> is used, the product is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol instead.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

When phenol reacts with dilute nitric acid, the two products are 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol.

State why 3-nitrophenol is not formed when phenol reacts with dilute nitric acid.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> 3-nitrophenol is not formed because:
> 
> - The –OH group is 2,4,6-directing (directs substitution to the 2, 4 and 6 positions) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The oxygen atom in the –OH group donates electron density into the benzene ring, increasing electron density at positions 2, 4 and 6. Electrophiles attack at these positions, not at position 3.

parts.problem_md:
Phenol, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH, has the following skeletal formula:

![Skeletal formula of phenol](assets/011-skeletal-formula-of-phenol.png)

If no reaction occurs, write **no reaction**.

Draw the skeletal formula of the organic product formed when phenol reacts with:

i) sodium

[1]

ii) sodium hydroxide

[1]

iii) ethanoic acid

[1]

iv) aqueous bromine

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) The product of phenol and sodium is:

![Structural equation showing phenol reacting with sodium to give sodium phenoxide and hydrogen gas](assets/012-structural-equation-showing-phenol-reacting-with.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct organic product: sodium phenoxide (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>ONa or C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>)

ii) The product of phenol and sodium hydroxide is:

![Structural equation showing phenol reacting with sodium hydroxide to give sodium phenoxide and water](assets/013-structural-equation-showing-phenol-reacting-with.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct organic product: sodium phenoxide (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>ONa)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) Phenol does not react with ethanoic acid **[1 mark]**

iv) The product of phenol and aqueous bromine is:

![Structural equation showing phenol reacting with bromine water to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol and hydrogen bromide](assets/014-structural-equation-showing-phenol-reacting-with.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for 2,4,6-tribromophenol
> 
> All three positions (2, 4, and 6) must be substituted with Br

> **[exam-tip]**
> Phenol is a weak acid so it will react with sodium metal to form the salt sodium phenoxide and hydrogen gas. You do not need to balance this equation for this mark.
> 
> Phenol will also react with a base such as NaOH to form the salt sodium phenoxide and water. You can show the negative charge on the oxygen and the positive charge on the sodium in sodium phenoxide.
> 
> Ethanoic acid is also a weak acid and no reaction will occur between phenol and ethanoic acid.
> 
> Phenol reacts with bromine water to form the tri-substituted compound 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

parts.problem_md: State the name of the reaction mechanism for the reaction of phenol with bromine water.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The name of the reaction mechanism for the reaction of phenol with bromine water is:
> 
> - Electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A lone pair of electrons on the oxygen atom overlaps with the delocalised π system of the benzene ring, increasing the electron density around the ring. This makes phenol particularly susceptible to attack by electrophiles, which is why it undergoes electrophilic substitution more readily than benzene.

parts.problem_md:
Phenol undergoes bromination when reacted with bromine water. Benzene also undergoes bromination but requires different conditions.

State the conditions needed for the bromination of phenol and the conditions needed for the bromination of benzene.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The conditions needed for the bromination of phenol and for the bromination of benzene are:
> 
> - Bromination of phenol: Room temperature **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Bromination of benzene: Pure bromine
> **AND**
> Aluminium bromide / AlBr<sub>3</sub> (catalyst) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A lone pair of electrons on the oxygen atom overlaps with the π bonding system of the benzene ring, increasing electron density in the ring. This makes phenol more susceptible to attack by electrophiles, so it reacts with bromine water at room temperature without a catalyst. Benzene requires pure bromine (rather than bromine water) and a halogen carrier catalyst such as AlBr<sub>3</sub>.

parts.problem_md:
Phenol is an aryl compound.

State the molecular formula of phenol.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The molecular formula of phenol is:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O
> **OR**
> C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> It helps to draw out the structure of phenol with all atoms shown to avoid miscounting hydrogen atoms. There are 5 hydrogens on the ring and 1 in the –OH group, giving 6H total: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O.

parts.problem_md:
Explain why phenol is a weak acid.

You should include an equation in your answer.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Phenol acts as a weak acid because:
> 
> - Phenol can donate the H atom from the O–H group to form the phenoxide ion **[1 mark]**
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
> **OR**
> C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH ⇌ C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> - The phenoxide ion is stable because the negative charge is delocalised (spread) over the entire ion **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Acids donate protons. Although phenol is a weak acid, it can still lose the H from the –OH group to form the phenoxide ion. The equilibrium lies to the left (phenol is not fully ionised), making it weakly acidic.

parts.problem_md: Describe and explain how the acidities of ethanol and phenol compare with that of water.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A comparison of the acidities of ethanol and phenol with that of water:
> 
> - Ethanol is less acidic than water **[1 mark]**
> - The ethyl group is electron-donating, concentrating more negative charge on the oxygen atom of the ethoxide ion **[1 mark]**
> - Phenol is more acidic than water **[1 mark]**
> - The phenoxide ion is more stable than hydroxide because the negative charge is delocalised over the ring **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order of acidity (least to most acidic): ethanol < water < phenol
> 
> In phenol, the phenoxide ion (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>) has its charge spread over the benzene ring via delocalisation. This reduces the tendency to accept H<sup>+</sup> back, making phenol more acidic than water.
> 
> In ethanol, the ethoxide ion (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>) has charge concentrated on oxygen because the ethyl group is electron-donating. The higher charge density means H<sup>+</sup> is more strongly attracted back, making ethanol less acidic than water.

parts.problem_md:
Phenol reacts with bromine water.

i) State the name of the product formed.

[1]

ii) Construct a balanced chemical equation for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the product formed when phenol reacts with bromine water is:
> 
> - 2,4,6-tribromophenol **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A balanced chemical equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - 3Br<sub>2</sub> + C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>2</sub>Br<sub>3</sub>OH + 3HBr **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The –OH group activates the benzene ring and directs substitution to positions 2, 4 and 6. Three bromine atoms substitute three hydrogen atoms. The product 2,4,6-tribromophenol forms as a white precipitate.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Phenol reacts with bromine water.

i) The name of the product formed when phenol reacts with bromine water is:
- 2,4,6-tribromophenol

ii) A balanced chemical equation for this reaction is:
- 3Br₂ + C₆H₅OH → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr

Compare the reagents and conditions required for the bromination of phenol and benzene. Use your answer to explain how these reactions show that phenol is more reactive than benzene.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A comparison showing that phenol is more reactive than benzene towards bromine:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Phenol reacts with bromine water (aqueous Br<sub>2</sub>) but benzene does not
> - Phenol trisubstitutes while benzene monosubstitutes
> - Benzene requires a halogen carrier catalyst (AlBr<sub>3</sub> / FeBr<sub>3</sub>) and pure bromine; phenol does not
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The –OH group in phenol increases the electron density of the ring, making it more reactive towards electrophiles. Phenol reacts under much milder conditions than benzene: no catalyst is needed and bromine water is sufficient.

parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The number of hybridised carbon atoms in phenyl 2-hydroxybenzoate:

> - sp = 0
> **AND**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), it can be helpful to highlight each carbon and identify its hybridisation.
> 
> In a benzene ring, all carbons are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised. The carbonyl carbon in an ester group (C=O) is also sp<sup>2</sup>.
> 
> Phenyl 2-hydroxybenzoate contains two benzene rings and one ester group, all with sp<sup>2</sup> carbons, so there are no sp or sp<sup>3</sup> carbons.

ii) The completed table showing reactions of phenyl 2-hydroxybenzoate is:

|---|---|---|
| Na | ![Structure of sodium 2-(phenoxycarbonyl)phenolate](assets/016-structure-of-sodium-2-phenoxycarbonyl-phenolate.png) | Acid-base reaction |

**[2 marks]**

> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of mesalamine

> **[exam-tip]**
> Mesalamine (5-aminosalicylic acid) has an –NH<sub>2</sub> group at position 5 and a –COOH group at position 1 (with –OH at position 2).
> 
> Compound X is the intermediate between salicylic acid and mesalamine. Step 1 introduces a nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>) at position 5 to give compound X (5-nitrosalicylic acid). Step 2 reduces the nitro group to give the amine in mesalamine.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A possible two step synthesis of mesalamine is shown below in Fig. 3.2.

Two-step synthesis pathway from salicylic acid to mesalamine via compound X, showing step 1 (nitration) and step 2 (reduction)

State the reagents and conditions required for steps **1** and **2** in Fig. 3.2 in part **(b)**.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents and conditions required for step **1** are:
> 
> - Dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Room temperature **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The reagents and conditions required for step **2** are:
> 
> - Sn / HCl **[1 mark]**
> - Heat under reflux **[1 mark]**
> - Excess NaOH (aq) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Step 1 is the nitration of salicylic acid. Unlike the nitration of benzene (which requires concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> and concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>), salicylic acid is more reactive because the –OH group is ring-activating. Dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> at room temperature is sufficient. The –COOH group is ring-deactivating, but the activating effect of the –OH dominates.
> 
> Step 2 converts the nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>) to an amine (–NH<sub>2</sub>) by reduction. Sn/HCl is the reducing agent and heat under reflux provides the energy. Under acidic conditions the amine product is protonated (–NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>), so excess NaOH is added in the final step to deprotonate it and give the free amine –NH<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problem_md:
This question is about the reactions of phenol and benzene.

Explain the difference in bromination of phenol and benzene. In your answer, include structures of any organic products formed in the reaction.
parts.solution_md:
The structure of 2,4,6-tribromophenol is:

![2,4,6-tribromophenol](assets/027-2-4-6-tribromophenol.jpeg)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of 2,4,6-tribromophenol
> 
> The difference in bromination of phenol and benzene, including structures of any organic products formed:
> 
> - Phenol has a lone pair on the oxygen atom that (partially) delocalises into the π system of the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> 
> - The π electrons of benzene are delocalised over the ring **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Phenol has a higher electron density in the ring than benzene **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Benzene cannot polarise the Br–Br bond
> **OR**
> Phenol can polarise the Br–Br bond (allow: δ<sup>+</sup> Br or Br<sup>+</sup> electrophile) **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Bromination of benzene requires a halogen carrier catalyst such as FeBr<sub>3</sub> / AlBr<sub>3</sub> and pure bromine **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature to form 2,4,6-tribromophenol **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question covers a lot of content. Break your answer into sections:
> 
> **Bromination of phenol**:
> 
> - The lone pair on the oxygen atom delocalises into the π ring, increasing electron density.
> - This allows phenol to polarise the Br–Br bond and react with bromine water at room temperature without a catalyst, giving 2,4,6-tribromophenol.
> 
> **Bromination of benzene**:
> 
> - The π electrons are delocalised but the electron density is lower than in phenol.
> - Benzene cannot polarise Br–Br on its own and requires pure bromine and a halogen carrier catalyst (FeBr<sub>3</sub> or AlBr<sub>3</sub>), giving bromobenzene.
> 
> **Directing effects**:
> 
> - The –OH group is an activating group that directs electrophiles to the 2, 4 and 6 positions, which is why three bromine atoms are substituted in phenol but only one in benzene.

parts.problem_md:
A mixture of 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol can be formed via the pathway shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Reaction pathway showing the nitration of phenol to form 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol](assets/028-reaction-pathway-showing-the-nitration-of-phenol.jpeg)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) State the reagents **and** conditions required for reaction **1**.

[1]

ii) Calculate the mass, in grams, of phenol required to form 30 g of 2-nitrophenol assuming a 35% yield. Give your answer to three significant figures and show your working.

mass = ............... g

[3]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents and conditions required for reaction **1** are:
> 
> - Dilute HNO<sub>3</sub>
> **AND**
> Room temperature **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the mass of phenol required to produce 30 g of 2-nitrophenol at 35% yield:

- State the M<sub>r</sub> values:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of 2-nitrophenol = 139.0

*M*<sub>r</sub> of phenol = 94.0

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the mass of 2-nitrophenol produced at 100% yield:

mass at 100% yield = $\frac{30}{35} \times 100$

mass at 100% yield = 85.71 g

- Calculate the moles of 2-nitrophenol:

moles = $\frac{85.71}{139.0}$

moles = 0.617 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Since the molar ratio of phenol : 2-nitrophenol = 1 : 1

moles of phenol = 0.617 mol

- Calculate the mass of phenol required:

mass = 0.617 x 94.0 = **58.0 g**

**[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The tricky part of this calculation is working back from the actual yield to find the theoretical mass at 100% yield. Rearrange the percentage yield formula: theoretical mass = actual mass ÷ % yield x 100.

parts.problem_md:
Phenol reacts with sodium to form a salt and hydrogen gas in an acid-base reaction.

Explain why phenol behaves as a weak acid.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Phenol behaves as a weak acid because:
> 
> - The O–H bond breaks; H<sup>+</sup> is donated and the phenoxide ion, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>, is formed **[1 mark]**
> - A lone pair on the oxygen atom (partially) delocalises into the π system of the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> - This stabilises the phenoxide ion / the negative charge is delocalised (spread) over the ring **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The delocalisation of the oxygen lone pair into the ring is the key difference between phenol and simple alcohols. It weakens the O–H bond compared to alcohols, making phenol acidic. However, phenol is still a weak acid because the equilibrium lies to the left, so it does not fully ionise in water.
> 
> The formula of the phenoxide ion is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>. The dissociation equation is:
> 
> C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH ⇌ C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup>
> 
> You may also be asked to calculate the pH of a phenol solution from a given concentration using the K<sub>a</sub> expression.
